clinicalPearls: A rare ovarian teratoma composed predominantly of mature thyroid tissue, classified as a monodermal teratoma
Most present as an incidental adnexal or pelvic mass rather than with thyroid symptoms
A minority secrete enough thyroid hormone to cause hyperthyroidism arising from ectopic ovarian tissue
Ectopic thyroid hormone production suppresses the eutopic thyroid, so neck radioiodine uptake is low while pelvic uptake may be demonstrable
It should be considered in unexplained thyrotoxicosis when the neck gland appears normal or shows suppressed uptake
Rarely it is associated with ascites and a raised tumour marker, mimicking ovarian malignancy
Malignant transformation into thyroid-type carcinoma can occur but is uncommon
Treatment is surgical removal of the affected ovary, with thyroid-directed management for any associated malignant histology
reference.pathophysiology: Struma ovarii is a germ-cell tumour of the ovary in which mature thyroid tissue forms the dominant or exclusive component. The ectopic thyroid follicular cells can retain the capacity to synthesise thyroid hormone, and when active in sufficient quantity they cause thyrotoxicosis independent of pituitary control, thereby suppressing thyroid-stimulating hormone and the normal cervical thyroid. Most tumours are benign, but the same follicular epithelium can rarely undergo malignant change resembling papillary or follicular thyroid carcinoma, with potential for spread. The mass itself may produce local pelvic symptoms or, uncommonly, ascites and pleural effusion.
additionalDifferentials: Graves disease or toxic nodular thyroid disease
Other functioning or non-functioning ovarian tumours
Mature cystic teratoma without significant thyroid tissue
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests demonstrating thyrotoxicosis when present
Radioiodine or radionuclide imaging showing suppressed neck uptake with pelvic uptake
Pelvic ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging of the adnexal mass
Tumour markers where ovarian malignancy is in the differential
Histological examination of the resected specimen
Thyroglobulin monitoring if malignant struma is identified
redFlags: Features suggesting malignant transformation or metastatic spread
Rapidly enlarging pelvic mass with ascites
Ovarian torsion of the tumour-bearing ovary
Unexplained thyrotoxicosis with a normal-appearing neck gland
reference.prognosis: The great majority are benign and cured by surgical removal, with resolution of any associated thyrotoxicosis; malignant struma ovarii is uncommon and generally indolent, though it warrants thyroid-cancer-style follow-up.
pitfalls: Attributing thyrotoxicosis solely to the neck thyroid and overlooking an ovarian source
Misinterpreting suppressed cervical radioiodine uptake without seeking a pelvic source
Assuming an adnexal mass with ascites is primary ovarian cancer
Failing to examine resected tissue for malignant thyroid histology
Neglecting thyroid-directed surveillance after removal of malignant struma
management: Definitive surgical resection of the ovarian tumour by cystectomy or oophorectomy, which is curative and resolves any associated thyrotoxicosis
Control thyrotoxic symptoms preoperatively with beta-blockade, adding antithyroid drugs where needed to render the patient euthyroid before surgery
Histological examination of the resected specimen to exclude malignant struma resembling papillary or follicular thyroid carcinoma
For malignant struma, consider completion total thyroidectomy to enable radioiodine ablation and thyroglobulin surveillance
Monitor thyroid function postoperatively to confirm resolution of the thyrotoxicosis
Long-term surveillance with thyroglobulin and imaging where malignant struma is identified
Multidisciplinary input from gynaecology and endocrinology, with endocrine oncology involvement if malignant
